analysis.one_liner: Bans surprise balance billing of patients in self-insured employer health plans for emergency and certain hospital services.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2019, never gained a single cosponsor, and died in the Senate Health Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop health care providers from "balance billing" — chasing patients for the difference between a provider's full charge and what their plan pays — in two situations: after emergency care, and when an out-of-network specialist treats them at a hospital that is in their network without the patient having a choice. It applies only to self-insured employer plans (plans where the employer itself pays the medical claims). Instead of billing the patient, providers would have to collect from the employer's plan, with unresolved payment disputes going to voluntary arbitration.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and their families covered by self-insured employer health plans — roughly the majority of people with employer coverage. Today, an out-of-network emergency room doctor or anesthesiologist can bill them for hundreds or thousands of dollars beyond their normal copay or deductible, even when the hospital itself was in-network. Under the bill, patients would owe only their usual in-network cost sharing, and the employer's plan would be solely responsible for paying the provider. Patients would also get a published list of which doctors are in-network and an annual warning about out-of-network billing risk.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers in self-insured employer health plans

how_it_helps.text: Patients in self-insured employer plans could no longer be billed for anything beyond their normal copay, coinsurance, or deductible for covered emergency services, even when the ER doctor or facility is out-of-network; the plan must treat out-of-network emergency care the same as in-network for cost sharing and must pay providers directly.

Patients treated by an out-of-network facility-based provider (for example, an anesthesiologist or radiologist) at an in-network hospital, where they had no chance to pick an in-network provider, could not be balance billed for the difference in rates.

Plans could not require prior authorization before pre-hospital emergency transport or treatment, and would have to publish a monthly-updated list of network providers and warn enrollees annually about the risk of out-of-network billing.

Disputes between providers and plans over payment would go to binding arbitration run by independent organizations with a three-year conflict-of-interest screen, rather than leaving providers to pursue patients directly.

analysis.who_pays: Self-insured employers, whose plans become solely liable for paying out-of-network emergency and facility-based providers instead of patients absorbing the difference. Out-of-network emergency physicians, hospitals, and facility-based specialists lose the revenue they currently collect by billing patients directly. The arbitration process would add dispute-resolution costs. To the extent plans end up paying providers' full claimed charges, employers' health costs could rise, which often shows up in wages or premium contributions over time.

drawbacks.text: The protection is narrow: it covers only self-insured group health plans, leaving people with fully insured plans — including individual market coverage and many workers at smaller employers — with no protection from surprise bills at all.

The payment benchmark favors providers: a plan must pay either the provider's own claimed amount, the provider's usual and customary community charge, or a negotiated amount — meaning the reference point is what the provider itself charges rather than an independent in-network benchmark, which could push plan costs up and be passed back to workers through premiums or wages.

The non-emergency protection applies only to facility-based providers at in-network facilities; patients can still be surprised by out-of-network billing in other circumstances the bill does not address, and the arbitration option is voluntary with minimum claim sizes of $3,000 for facility services and $500 for professional services, leaving smaller disputes to the plan and provider to settle between themselves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection — a patient cannot be chased for a surprise emergency bill — is real and directly addresses a problem that harms many families, but the bill is a partial fix. It leaves out everyone in fully insured plans, and its payment formula (pay the provider's claim or its own usual charges) is written so providers have little pressure to accept less, meaning employers and ultimately workers would likely absorb higher costs. A stronger version would use an independent benchmark for out-of-network payment and cover all plan types.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Rick Scott of Florida introduced the bill on May 1, 2019; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No other senator joined as a cosponsor at any point during the two-year Congress.
The committee took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and it never reached the Senate floor before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Out-of-network emergency physicians, hospitals, and facility-based specialists kept the ability to balance bill patients in self-insured plans, and self-insured employers were spared new payment obligations. Patients were not left with nothing overall — Congress passed a broader surprise-billing ban (the No Surprises Act) in December 2020 as part of a year-end spending law — but this bill itself died without moving.

for.name: Sen. Rick Scott
for.role: U.S. Senator from Florida, sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; it was his only cosponsor-less health billing measure and he recruited no colleagues to join it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (chair: Sen. Lamar Alexander)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or committee vote; the bill sat in committee from May 2019 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a single Republican senator with zero cosponsors from either party, and no vote of any kind was ever recorded, so no partisan split exists in the record.

industries.industry: Emergency physicians and facility-based specialists (ER staffing, anesthesiology, radiology)
industries.note: These providers earn a large share of revenue by billing out-of-network patients directly for the gap between their charges and plan payments. The bill would make self-insured plans solely liable and bar providers from billing patients, cutting off that revenue stream.

Facilities would lose the right to collect balance bills from self-insured plan members for emergency services, and their facility-based providers would be restricted at in-network hospitals. Because these bills land on patients at their most vulnerable moments, the industry's interest here runs against patients' financial security.

Employers would take on full liability for out-of-network emergency and facility-based claims, and the bill's payment options (the provider's claim or its usual charges) give providers leverage to charge more — costs that tend to return to workers as premiums or slower wage growth. At the same time, employees would no longer face catastrophic surprise bills.
The bill would create a new government-contracted market for organizations with five or more years of experience as neutral arbiters to resolve plan-provider payment disputes.
